source_document: Document 4 — Edward Baines on England's position

left.label: Document 4 — Baines says Britain's island location and its command of the seas kept it safe from invasion

right.label: In 1805, Britain's Royal Navy defeated the French and Spanish fleets at Trafalgar (OI). Edward Baines wrote that Britain's island location, together with its command of the seas, kept it safe from invasion (Doc 4).

rationale.a: Trafalgar is nowhere in Document 4. Baines says Britain commanded the seas; the battle shows how it won that command. Setting the scene first is what makes the fact do work. (This is the example from Day 2's OI box. Baines's source gives no year, so his sentence has none.)

documents.source_document: Document 4 — Edward Baines on England's position
documents.source_citation: Source: Edward Baines, History of the Cotton Manufacture in Great Britain, A. M. Kelley
documents.source_text: In comparing the advantages of England for manufactures with those of other countries, we can by no means overlook the excellent commercial position of the country — intermediate between the north and south of Europe; and its insular situation [island location], which, combined with the command of the seas, secures our territory from invasion or annoyance. The German ocean, the Baltic, and the Mediterranean are the regular highways for our ships; and our western ports command an unobstructed [clear] passage to the Atlantic, and to every quarter [part] of the world.
